_readme: Facts the PUBLISHED policies assert that live outside this repository — in the
Supabase dashboard, in the production database, or with a provider. Nothing in the
build or the type system can see any of them, so an inaccurate statement here is
invisible until a regulator reads the page. `npm run check:claims` fails while a
published page makes one of these claims and the matching entry is unverified.
Set `verified` to the ISO date you CHECKED it, not the date you intended to. That
date is the evidence; a tick with no date is a guess. Re-verify anything that could
have drifted (a plan change, a provider migration, someone toggling a setting).
`expires` (optional) is for a claim that is true today but stops being true on a
knowable date unless someone acts, or that could silently drift and should be
re-checked on a cadence. check:claims FAILS once the date passes while the claim is
still published — so a deadline lives in the gate rather than in a prose note beside
a green tick, which is the same silent failure this file exists to prevent.

db_region_ireland.expiresWhy: Six-monthly re-check. A project migration or a provider region change would not announce itself, and the whole Art. 44-49 position rests on this one fact.
db_region_ireland.claim: Account and app data is stored in Ireland (eu-west-1).
db_region_ireland.why: The whole Art. 44-49 position rests on it. If the region is not in the EEA, every transfer statement in both documents is wrong and an Art. 46 safeguard is required that is not in place.
db_region_ireland.howToVerify: Supabase dashboard -> Project Settings -> General -> Region.

static_host_github_pages.expiresWhy: Six-monthly re-check. GitHub's EU-US Data Privacy Framework self-certification can lapse, and moving the static host would invalidate the recipient, country and transfer-mechanism disclosures in both documents at once.
static_host_github_pages.claim: The app's static files are served by GitHub Pages (GitHub, Inc., United States); EEA transfers rely on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework and the SCCs in GitHub's Data Protection Agreement.
static_host_github_pages.why: PRIVACY.md s.6/s.10 and the consumer-health notice now name GitHub, Inc. as the host, the United States as the country of processing, and DPF+SCCs as the Art. 46 safeguard. All three are facts about an outside provider no build step can observe; if GitHub drops its DPF certification or the app moves host, the published transfer basis is wrong while every page still renders.
static_host_github_pages.howToVerify: Confirm the deployed origin is GitHub Pages (repo Settings -> Pages). Confirm GitHub, Inc. is still on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework list at dataprivacyframework.gov, and that GitHub's current Data Protection Agreement (github.com/customer-terms/github-data-protection-agreement) still incorporates the 2021/914 Standard Contractual Clauses. Verified 2026-10-21 against GitHub's Trust Center, General Privacy Statement and the GitHub Pages 'Data collection' note (visitor IPs logged for security; no published retention period).

leaked_password_protection.note: 2026-08-05: HaveIBeenPwned leaked-password protection is a Supabase Pro-plan feature; the project is on the free plan (Management API PATCH returns HTTP 402). The claim was therefore REMOVED from legal/PRIVACY.md § 8 rather than left unbacked — check:claims no longer requires it. To restore the claim, upgrade to Pro, enable Auth -> Passwords -> leaked password protection, re-add the sentence, and set verified here.
leaked_password_protection.claim: New passwords are checked against known breached-password lists.
leaked_password_protection.why: PRIVACY.md § 8 states it as a fact about the running service, in the section a regulator reads first. It is a dashboard toggle: the app cannot enforce or detect it.
leaked_password_protection.howToVerify: Auth -> Sign In / Providers -> Passwords -> leaked password protection ON. Then re-run the Supabase security advisor: `auth_leaked_password_protection` must no longer appear.

min_password_length_server.claim: New passwords must be at least 10 characters.
min_password_length_server.why: MIN_PASSWORD enforces this in the client only. A request straight to the auth API bypasses the client, so the server minimum is the real gate and the one the sentence describes.
min_password_length_server.howToVerify: Auth -> Sign In / Providers -> Passwords -> minimum length = 10 (must match MIN_PASSWORD in src/gym-tracker-app.tsx).

secure_email_change.claim: An email change is confirmed from both the old and the new address.
secure_email_change.why: With 'Secure email change' off, one confirmation on the NEW address is enough — so anyone with a borrowed unlocked device could move the account to their own inbox, and § 9's promise would be false. Note the claim is made in TWO places: PRIVACY.md § 9 (which check:claims scans, via the built page) and the in-app success message in SettingsScreen ('we sent a confirmation link to your old and new address'), which no gate can see because check:claims reads public/*.html only. If this setting is ever turned off, both have to change.
secure_email_change.howToVerify: Auth -> Emails -> Secure email change ON. Then check the in-app copy in src/gym-tracker-app.tsx still matches.

consents_table_live.claim: The consent record is stored in a table the user cannot alter or delete from.
consents_table_live.phrase: a table you cannot alter or delete from
consents_table_live.why: Until migration 0004 is applied the only consent record is the user-writable auth metadata copy — which is exactly the Art. 7(1) gap the table closes. The app feature-detects the table and stays silent while it is absent, so nothing fails; the claim just is not true. The wording is deliberately narrowed to what 0004 delivers against the threat it was built for (a user rewriting their own consent timestamp): the service_role key bypasses RLS entirely, and § 8 already tells the reader the operator reaches the database through the admin console, so an unqualified 'cannot be altered by anyone' would have been overstated. See consents_immutable_trigger for the insert side.
consents_table_live.howToVerify: Run supabase/migrations/0004_add_consents_table.sql, then confirm `update public.consents set granted_at = now();` ERRORS (no UPDATE policy).

auth_log_purge_available.claim: The mechanism that enforces the 90-day sign-in-log retention exists in production.
auth_log_purge_available.why: Half of the § 7 claim, split out from auth_log_purge_scheduled so the half that IS done is not carrying the half that is not. Not published on its own — the published sentence needs both halves.
auth_log_purge_available.howToVerify: Migration 0005 applied to prod 2026-08-05: public.purge_auth_audit_log() present, SECURITY DEFINER, EXECUTE granted to service_role only (not authenticated/anon).

auth_log_purge_scheduled.expiresWhy: Six-monthly re-check that the scheduled purge is still recurring. A pg_cron job can silently stop — extension disabled, job deactivated, or a nightly error that looks identical to success in cron.job — so re-confirm cron.job_run_details still shows recent status='succeeded' runs for 'purge-auth-audit-log'.
auth_log_purge_scheduled.note: 2026-10-23: APPLIED and verified. Migration 0008 installed pg_cron 1.6.4 (in pg_catalog, not public) and scheduled job 'purge-auth-audit-log' daily at 03:17 UTC running `select public.purge_auth_audit_log(90, false)`. The evidence is a succeeded SCHEDULED run, not merely a registered job (a job that errors nightly is indistinguishable from a working one in cron.job): cron.job_run_details showed status='succeeded' at 2026-10-23 18:30:00 UTC, produced by temporarily setting the schedule to every-minute and then reverting it to daily. auth.audit_log_entries held 0 rows older than 90 days at the time, so this run was a clean no-op delete — the mechanism is proven and will delete for real as entries age past 90 days. Applied via the Supabase Management API using SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN, because the project's MCP runs --read-only (connects as supabase_read_only_user, which cannot CREATE in public or DELETE auth.audit_log_entries). See auth_log_purge_available for the 0005 half.
auth_log_purge_scheduled.claim: The provider's sign-in security log is kept for 90 days — i.e. we purge it on that schedule.
auth_log_purge_scheduled.why: auth.audit_log_entries has no FK to auth.users and survives account deletion. The retention only exists if migration 0005 is applied AND the purge actually recurs — which is now migration 0008's pg_cron job rather than an operator running `npm run purge:auth-log -- --purge` by hand. Either way the failure mode is silence: nothing anywhere goes red when the purge simply stops happening, which is why this claim is gated here with a deadline.
auth_log_purge_scheduled.howToVerify: Applied and verified 2026-10-23. To RE-verify: `select status, start_time from cron.job_run_details where jobid = (select jobid from cron.job where jobname = 'purge-auth-audit-log') order by start_time desc limit 1;` must show a recent status='succeeded', and `cron.job` must still list the job active on '17 3 * * *'. A registered job that errors every night is indistinguishable from a working one in `cron.job`, so the run record is the evidence, not the schedule. Running `npm run purge:auth-log -- --purge` by hand remains fine for an ad-hoc purge, but it is no longer what the published sentence depends on.

consents_immutable_trigger.note: 2026-10-23: APPLIED (migration 0007, via the Supabase Management API). Trigger consents_stamp_trg is live on public.consents; consents_stamp() is SECURITY DEFINER with search_path=''. Verified functionally (rolled back, no persisted test row): a client-sent recorded_at of '2000-01-01' was stored as now() (year 2026), and a granted_at two days in the future was refused with 'consents.granted_at is in the future'. Still published:[] — PRIVACY.md § 3's wording was narrowed to what 0004 alone delivers, so no gate rides on this; the tick records that the stronger guarantee now exists should the wording be strengthened again.
consents_immutable_trigger.claim: The consent record's server-side timestamps cannot be set by the client.
consents_immutable_trigger.phrase: cannot be rewritten after the fact
consents_immutable_trigger.why: Migration 0004's append-only RLS stops a row being UPDATEd; it does not stop a backdated row being INSERTed, because a column DEFAULT applies only when the client omits the column. 0007 adds the BEFORE INSERT trigger that makes recorded_at genuinely the server's. Not published on its own — PRIVACY.md § 3 was narrowed to what 0004 alone actually delivers, so this entry has nothing riding on it until the wording is strengthened again.
consents_immutable_trigger.howToVerify: Applied 2026-10-23. To re-verify: confirm trigger consents_stamp_trg exists on public.consents, and (in a rolled-back transaction) that an insert carrying recorded_at = '2000-01-01' still stores now() and that granted_at two days in the future is refused.
